blocks.text:
A running process cannot hold a disk, a socket or a terminal directly. The operating system therefore offers one narrow abstraction for all of them: the file, accessed through a small integer called a file descriptor. A Spring Boot service uses this abstraction for the jar it was started from, every log line, every configuration file, every HTTP connection and every database connection. Exhausting or misconfiguring the abstraction produces some of the most common production failures: `Too many open files`, `Permission denied` after a deployment and disks that are full for no visible reason. This chapter defines the model precisely, so that the incidents at the end of the chapter can be diagnosed from first principles.

### Concept and mechanism

#### The file abstraction

In UNIX-derived systems a file is a sequence of bytes that supports a small set of operations: `open`, `read`, `write`, `lseek`, `close`, plus `fsync`, `mmap` and `ioctl` for special purposes. The kernel does not care whether the bytes live on a disk, in memory or on the far side of a network connection. Regular files, directories, symbolic links, character devices (`/dev/null`), block devices (`/dev/vda`), pipes, sockets and the pseudo files of `/proc` all use the same descriptor interface. The type of an object is the first character of the `ls -l` mode string: `-` regular file, `d` directory, `l` symbolic link, `c` character device, `b` block device, `p` named pipe, `s` socket.

#### Three tables between a descriptor and the data

A file descriptor is only an index. Between the index and the stored data lie three kernel structures, and the difference between them explains the behaviour of `dup`, `fork` and shared log files.

rows: index (0, 1, 2, ...) to open file description, plus the close-on-exec flag
current offset, access mode (`O_RDONLY`, `O_RDWR`), status flags (`O_APPEND`, `O_NONBLOCK`), pointer to the inode
one per file object on a file system
type, owner, mode, size, timestamps, link count, location of the data blocks
blocks.caption: The three levels of the open-file model.

blocks.text: Every successful `open` creates a new OFD and installs it in the lowest free slot of the descriptor table. The call `dup(fd)` installs a second slot that points to the same OFD, and `fork` copies the whole descriptor table, so parent and child share every OFD. Two descriptors that share an OFD share the offset: a write through one moves the position seen by the other. Two independent `open` calls on the same path create two OFDs with independent offsets, although both reach the same inode.

blocks.text:
#### Standard descriptors and redirection

Descriptor 0 is standard input, 1 is standard output and 2 is standard error. These numbers are conventions inherited across `fork` and `execve`, not special kernel objects. The shell implements the redirection `ls /nonexistent > out.txt` `2>&1` by opening the file after `fork` and before `execve`, then copying the descriptor onto slots 1 and 2 with `dup2`. The program that is executed afterwards writes to descriptor 2 without knowing that it leads to a file. Pipelines work in the same way, with `pipe` supplying the two ends; the chapter on inter-process communication in the Part on processes, threads and scheduling shows the pipe case.

blocks.text:
The descriptor flag `FD_CLOEXEC` (set with `O_CLOEXEC` at open time) closes a descriptor automatically during `execve`. Well-behaved programs set this flag on files and sockets so that child processes do not inherit them; the JDK additionally closes inherited descriptors above 2 in a child started through `ProcessBuilder`. A child that does inherit a listening socket or a log file can keep it open after the parent has closed it, which later appears as a deleted-but-open file or a port that cannot be rebound.

#### Observing descriptors through /proc

For any process, `/proc/PID/fd` contains one symbolic link per open descriptor, and `/proc/PID/fdinfo/N` reports the OFD state: the current offset (`pos`), the octal flags, the mount identifier and the inode number. These two views are the primary diagnostic interface for descriptor leaks, because they require no agent and work for any process owned by the inspecting user. The symbolic link target shows the path, `socket:[inode]`, `pipe:[inode]` or `anon_inode:[eventpoll]` for epoll instances.

#### Limits on open files

Three independent limits apply, and a failure message does not say which one was reached.

- The per-process soft limit (`RLIMIT_NOFILE`, shown by `ulimit -Sn`) is the value against which `open` and `socket` return `EMFILE`, reported by Java as `Too many open files`.
- The per-process hard limit (`ulimit -Hn`) is the ceiling to which an unprivileged process may raise its own soft limit. The kernel parameter `fs.nr_open` bounds the hard limit itself.
- The system-wide limit `fs.file-max` bounds the total number of open file descriptions on the machine; exceeding it returns `ENFILE`. The file `/proc/sys/fs/file-nr` shows the allocated count, the unused count and the maximum.

On the build machine the kernel reported `fs.nr_open = 1048576`, `fs.file-max = 819675`, a soft and hard limit of 20000 for the shell, and `fs.file-nr` of `132 0 819675`. The HotSpot flag `-XX:+MaxFDLimit` is enabled by default and raises the soft limit to the hard limit when the JVM starts. The experiment later in this chapter confirmed it: a process started with a soft limit of 256 and a hard limit of 4096 reported a soft limit of 4096 inside the JVM.

**Layers that bound open files, from outermost to innermost**

Kernel hard ceiling: fs.nr\_open = 1048576 per process (observed)

System-wide: fs.file-max = 819675 (observed); fs.file-nr shows allocated / unused / max

PAM / limits.conf or systemd DefaultLimitNOFILE: sets the hard limit of login sessions and services

Unit file: LimitNOFILE=65536 (systemd) or --ulimit nofile=65536:65536 (Docker) or runtime default

Soft limit of the process: ulimit -n (observed 20000 here) = what EMFILE is raised against

JVM: -XX:+MaxFDLimit (default true) raises the soft limit to the hard limit at start (observed 256 -\> 4096)

*Figure 5.3. The limits form layers from the kernel ceiling down to the JVM; an* `EMFILE` *error is raised against the innermost soft limit,* *but the value must be set in whichever outer layer starts the process.*

#### Permissions, umask and special bits

Each inode stores an owner uid, a group gid and a 12-bit mode. The nine permission bits form three classes: owner, group and other. The kernel selects exactly one class for a given process: owner if the effective uid matches, otherwise group if the effective gid or a supplementary group matches, otherwise other. The selected class is the only one consulted, so an owner with mode `0044` cannot read the file even though group and other can. The root user bypasses these checks through the capabilities `CAP_DAC_OVERRIDE` and `CAP_DAC_READ_SEARCH`.

For a directory the bits mean: `r` list names, `w` create, delete or rename entries (this requires `x` as well), `x` traverse the directory to reach entries inside. Deleting a file therefore depends on the permission of the directory, not of the file. The sticky bit on a directory (`/tmp` has mode `1777`) restricts deletion to the owner of the file or of the directory.

`open`*, so a requested 0666 becomes 0644 under umask 022.*

The special bits change who a process runs as. The setuid bit makes an executable run with the uid of its owner: on the build machine `/usr/bin/passwd` has mode `-rwsr-xr-x` and owner root, so any user can change a password entry that only root can write. The setgid bit on a directory makes new files inherit the directory group, which shared deployment directories use. Access control lists extend the owner, group and other triplets with entries for named users and groups, managed with `setfacl` and `getfacl`; the build machine had neither tool installed, so ACL syntax is not demonstrated here.

### Worked trace: one file, three descriptors

The C program in the listing opens `data.txt` twice, duplicates the first descriptor, writes ten bytes, forks, lets the child write three more bytes and prints the offsets. Each step corresponds to a row in the figure above.

blocks.title: fdtable.c

blocks.code:
$ gcc -Wall -o fdtable fdtable.c && ./fdtable
fd1    fd=3 offset=10
fd2    fd=4 offset=0
fd3    fd=5 offset=10
parent fd=3 offset=13
total 0
lrwx------ 1 root root 64 Oct 18 02:15 3 -> /tmp/osw_o5/c/data.txt
lr-x------ 1 root root 64 Oct 18 02:15 4 -> /tmp/osw_o5/c/data.txt
lrwx------ 1 root root 64 Oct 18 02:15 5 -> /tmp/osw_o5/c/data.txt
pos:    13
flags:  0100002
mnt_id: 28
ino:    966895
$ cat data.txt
ABCDEFGHIJxyz
blocks.title: Compile and run (standard descriptors 0 to 2 omitted from the listing)

blocks.text:
The numbered interpretation follows.

1. The three `open`/`dup` calls take the lowest free slots 3, 4 and 5, because 0 to 2 are occupied.
2. After the ten-byte write through descriptor 3, descriptors 3 and 5 report offset 10 because they share one OFD; descriptor 4 reports 0 because it owns a separate OFD.
3. The `fork` copies the table. The child writes `xyz` through its copy of descriptor 3, which points to the same OFD, so the shared offset advances from 10 to 13 and the parent observes 13 without having written anything.
4. The file contains `ABCDEFGHIJxyz`: the child appended after the parent data instead of overwriting it. This is the behaviour that lets a shell script and its children write one log file in sequence.
5. `fdinfo` confirms `pos: 13` and the flags `0100002`, which is octal for `O_RDWR` (2) together with `O_LARGEFILE` (0100000).

### Hands-on

#### Redirection under strace

The following session traces the shell while it executes a redirected command. The trace was filtered to the calls that matter; the process identifiers are typical.

blocks.code:
$ strace -f -e trace=openat,dup2,close,execve -o st.txt bash -c 'ls /nonexistent > out.txt 2>&1'
$ grep -E 'out.txt|dup2|execve' st.txt
4791  execve("/usr/bin/bash", ["bash", "-c", "ls /nonexistent > out.txt 2>&1"], ...) = 0
4792  openat(AT_FDCWD, "out.txt", O_WRONLY|O_CREAT|O_TRUNC, 0666) = 3
4792  dup2(3, 1)                        = 1
4792  dup2(1, 2)                        = 2
4792  execve("/usr/bin/ls", ["ls", "/nonexistent"], ...) = 0
$ cat out.txt
ls: cannot access '/nonexistent': No such file or directory
blocks.title: The shell opens, duplicates and executes

blocks.text:
The order of the redirections matters. In `> out.txt 2>&1` descriptor 2 is copied from descriptor 1 after descriptor 1 already points to the file, so both reach the file. In `2>&1 > out.txt` descriptor 2 is copied first and still points to the terminal or pipe; error output then bypasses the file. Container log collection depends on this: a service whose error stream is not redirected to the same destination as its output loses stack traces.

#### Permissions and umask

blocks.code:
$ umask
0022
$ setpriv --reuid=1000 --regid=1000 --clear-groups bash -c 'touch data/f2; ls -ln data/f2'
-rw-r--r-- 1 1000 1000 0 Oct 18 02:19 data/f2
$ (umask 077; touch data/private; ls -ln data/private)
-rw------- 1 0 0 0 Oct 18 02:19 data/private
$ setpriv --reuid=1001 --regid=1001 --clear-groups bash -c 'cat data/private'
cat: data/private: Permission denied

#### Descriptors of a JVM

A JVM that serves many connections holds one socket descriptor per connection in addition to its jar, class library image and log files. The server in the chapter on I/O models held the following after 500 clients connected (typical output):

blocks.code:
$ ls /proc/$JP/fd | wc -l
508
$ ls -l /proc/$JP/fd | grep -E "eventpoll|socket" | awk '{print $NF}' \
    | sed 's/\[.*//' | sort | uniq -c
      1 anon_inode:
    502 socket:
blocks.title: Descriptors of the NioEcho JVM with 500 connected clients

blocks.text:
### Real-world incidents

#### Incident: Too many open files caused by a descriptor leak

**Scenario.** A Spring Boot service on Kubernetes reads a small tenant configuration file for every request through a helper that opens a `FileInputStream` and never closes it. The container runs with the default limit of 1024 descriptors on some runtimes and 1048576 on others; this instance had a soft limit of 20000 in production and was started with 256 in the reproduction below.

**Symptoms.** After several hours the error rate rises abruptly. Logs contain `java.io.IOException: ... (Too many` `open files)` for unrelated operations such as accepting HTTP connections, opening database sockets and writing logs. The readiness probe fails because the server cannot accept the probe connection. Heap usage and CPU are normal.

**Diagnosis.** The first step compares the current descriptor count with the limit of the process. The second classifies the descriptors by target, which identifies the leak source. The reproduction used `FdLeak.java` (listing below) under `ulimit` `-n 256`.

blocks.title: FdLeak.java

blocks.code:
$ (ulimit -n 256; java FdLeak.java > leak.out 2>&1 &)
$ cat leak.out
call 253 failed: /etc/hostname (Too many open files)
pid 3327, leaked streams: 252
$ grep "open files" /proc/3327/limits
Max open files            256                  256                  files
$ ls /proc/3327/fd | wc -l
256
$ ls -l /proc/3327/fd | awk '{print $NF}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -3
    252 /etc/hostname
      2 /tmp/osw_o5/j/leak.out
      1 /usr/lib/jvm/java-21-openjdk-amd64/lib/modules
$ java FdLeak.java fixed
all calls succeeded; open descriptors: 5
blocks.title: Reproduction and diagnosis (output from the build machine)

blocks.text: The count equals the limit (256), and 252 of the descriptors point to the same path. Descriptors pointing to one path indicate an unclosed file stream. If the majority were `socket:[...]`, the next commands would be `ss -tanp` to count connection states per remote address and `lsof -i -a -p PID` to identify the peer, which usually reveals a client library whose responses are not closed. The failing call is a symptom; the leak site is wherever the stream was created.

blocks.text:
**Root cause.** A code path obtained a descriptor and kept a reference without closing it. The garbage collector does not close descriptors promptly: finalisation is not guaranteed, and a heap with plenty of free space may not collect for a long time, so the leak is invisible to heap monitoring.

**Fix.** Immediate mitigation: restart the process to release the descriptors, and raise the limit temporarily only if restarts are impossible. Permanent fix: close every stream with try-with-resources, as in `readConfigFixed`, and reuse HTTP clients (for example one `HttpClient` or `RestTemplate` per application) rather than creating one per request.

**Prevention.** Export the descriptor count as a metric (Micrometer publishes `process.files.open` and `process.files.max`) and alert at 80 percent of the soft limit. A leak appears as a straight rising line, a legitimately busy server as a plateau. Add a load test that checks the count after traffic stops.

blocks.text:
#### Incident: file descriptor limit too low in systemd or a container

**Scenario.** A service works on a developer machine and in a staging container but fails under load in production after migration to a systemd unit. The shell limit on the host is 20000, so the team assumes the same value applies to the service.

**Symptoms.** `Too many open files` appears at only about 1000 concurrent connections, far below the shell limit. Increasing `fs.file-max` has no effect.

**Diagnosis.** The limit of a running process is read from the process, never from the shell that was used to log in. The reproduction below shows that the limit follows the process and its parent chain.

blocks.code:
$ (ulimit -n 1024; sleep 60 & echo $! > sl.pid)
$ grep "open files" /proc/$(cat sl.pid)/limits
Max open files            1024                 1024                 files
$ prlimit --pid $(cat sl.pid) --nofile=65536:65536
prlimit: failed to set the NOFILE resource limit: Operation not permitted
$ cat /proc/sys/fs/nr_open /proc/sys/fs/file-max
1048576
819675
blocks.title: The limit belongs to the process that was started with it

blocks.text:
The second command failed on the build machine because the container that hosts it lacks the capability `CAP_SYS_RESOURCE`; on an ordinary host, root can raise the limit of a live process with `prlimit`, which is useful as a mitigation. The decisive diagnostic is `grep "open files" /proc/PID/limits` against the production process, which here would show the value 1024 or 4096 granted by the service manager, not 20000.

**Root cause.** The limit was configured in the layer that does not apply: shell profiles and `limits.conf` do not affect services started by systemd, which applies `LimitNOFILE` from the unit or from `DefaultLimitNOFILE` in `system.conf`. In container platforms the limit comes from the container runtime defaults.

**Fix.** Set the limit in the layer that starts the process (typical configuration, not run on the build machine because systemd is not the init system there):

**/etc/systemd/system/orders.service.d/limits.conf**

blocks.code:
[Service]
LimitNOFILE=65536

blocks.text:
For Docker use `docker run --ulimit nofile=65536:65536`; for Kubernetes the limit is inherited from the container runtime configuration of the node and is raised through the runtime, not through the pod specification. After the change, restart the service and verify the new value in `/proc/PID/limits`.

**Prevention.** Document the limit as part of the service definition, log `ulimit -n` at application start and publish `process.files.max` as a metric next to `process.files.open`. Size the limit from the connection budget: each client connection consumes one descriptor, each upstream connection one more, plus database pool size, log files and a safety margin.

#### Incident: Permission denied after a deployment

**Scenario.** A hardened image replaces a base image that ran as root. The new image declares `USER 1000` and the pod sets `runAsNonRoot: true`. The service writes a lock file and temporary uploads to a mounted volume that was created earlier by the old image.

**Symptoms.** The new pods start, but every upload fails with `java.nio.file.AccessDeniedException:` `/data/app.lock`. The old pods continued to work with the same volume.

**Diagnosis.** The numeric identity of the process is compared with the numeric owner and mode of the directory. Names can be misleading because the same uid may map to different names in different images; `ls -ln` and `id` show numbers.

blocks.code:
$ ls -ldn data
drwxr-xr-x 2 0 0 4096 Oct 18 02:19 data
$ setpriv --reuid=1000 --regid=1000 --clear-groups bash -c 'touch data/app.lock; echo rc=$?'
touch: cannot touch 'data/app.lock': Permission denied
rc=1
$ chown 1000:1000 data
$ setpriv --reuid=1000 --regid=1000 --clear-groups \
    bash -c 'touch data/app.lock && echo created; ls -ln data'
created
total 0
-rw-r--r-- 1 1000 1000 0 Oct 18 02:19 app.lock
blocks.title: Reproduction with a root-owned directory (run as root; setpriv drops to uid 1000)

blocks.text:
The directory belongs to uid 0 with mode `755`, so uid 1000 falls in the "other" class, which has no write bit. Searching for the cause in application code would be wasted effort; the kernel returned `EACCES` from `openat`, and `strace -f -e` `trace=openat -p PID` would show it with the exact path.

**Root cause.** The image changed the runtime uid but the volume kept the ownership assigned under the previous uid.

**Fix.** Immediate: change ownership of the volume contents to the new uid (an init container running `chown -R` `1000:1000 /data`). Permanent: in Kubernetes set `securityContext.fsGroup: 1000` so that the kubelet makes the volume group-owned by gid 1000 and group-writable; in Docker use a matching `--user` and a host directory with the same owner. Setting mode `777` or reverting to root removes the symptom while removing the isolation that motivated the change.

**Prevention.** Run the hardened image in staging with the real volume type. Include a startup self-test that creates and deletes a file in each writable directory and fails fast with a message naming the uid, the path and the mode. Keep the `umask` of the image consistent: with `umask 077` in a base image, files created by one container are unreadable to a backup or sidecar container that runs under another uid.

blocks.text:
### Questions to expect

#### What is the difference between a file descriptor, an open file description and an inode?

A descriptor is a per-process integer index. It points to an open file description, a system-wide structure holding the offset and the open flags. The description points to the inode, which stores the file metadata and the location of the data. `dup` and `fork` create several descriptors for one description (shared offset); two `open` calls create two descriptions for one inode.

#### What happens to descriptors on fork and on execve?

`fork` duplicates the descriptor table, so parent and child share the open file descriptions. `execve` keeps the descriptors except those with the close-on-exec flag. The shell relies on this to implement redirection and pipelines.

#### How does the shell implement `command > file 2>&1`?

After `fork` the child opens the file, which receives descriptor 3, then `dup2(3, 1)` and `dup2(1, 2)` make descriptors 1 and 2 refer to it, and the child executes the command. The order is significant: `2>&1 > file` would copy the original destination of descriptor 1 to descriptor 2 first.

#### Why can a process hit `Too many open files` when the system limit is far from reached?

The error refers to the per-process soft limit, `RLIMIT_NOFILE`, not to `fs.file-max`. The soft limit is inherited from the parent or set by the service manager (`LimitNOFILE`) or container runtime, so a shell limit of 20000 does not apply to a systemd service.

#### How is a descriptor leak found in a running JVM?

Compare `ls /proc/PID/fd | wc -l` with `/proc/PID/limits`, then group the link targets with `ls -l /proc/PID/fd |` `awk '{print $NF}' | sort | uniq -c`. Many identical file paths indicate unclosed streams; many `socket:` entries indicate unclosed connections, which `ss -tanp` and `lsof -i` attribute to remote peers.

#### Can a user delete a file that the user cannot write?

Yes, if the user has write and execute permission on the containing directory, because deletion modifies the directory entry. The sticky bit (for example on `/tmp`) restricts deletion to the owner of the file or directory.

#### What does the umask do?

The umask removes permission bits from the mode requested at creation. A requested mode of 0666 under umask 022 becomes 0644; a directory requested with 0777 becomes 0755. It does not alter existing files.

#### What does setuid do and why is it dangerous?

A setuid executable runs with the effective uid of its owner instead of the caller. It allows controlled privilege escalation (for example `passwd`), but any flaw in the program becomes a privilege escalation flaw, so setuid binaries are kept few and small; capabilities offer a narrower alternative.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
Key points

- A descriptor indexes a per-process table; open file descriptions are shared by `dup` and `fork` and carry the offset and flags; inodes carry the metadata.
- Redirection is `dup2` between `fork` and `execve`; the order of redirections changes the result.
- Three limits bound open files: the soft limit (`EMFILE`), the hard limit and `fs.file-max` (`ENFILE`); the limit of a service comes from its starter, not from the login shell.
- `/proc/PID/fd` and `/proc/PID/limits` diagnose leaks without tools; descriptors with identical targets point to the leak site.
- Permission checks use exactly one class (owner, group or other) and directory bits govern name operations; numeric uids decide, not names.

A disk is an array of fixed-size blocks without names, ownership or structure. A file system imposes the structure that makes it usable: it maps names to files, files to blocks, tracks free space, enforces permissions and survives power failure without corrupting itself. The design decisions of the file system explain behaviours that production engineers meet daily: why the disk can be full while `du` shows little, why deleting a log file does not free space, why a crash does not destroy a database that used `fsync` and why a container can modify a read-only image.

### Concept and mechanism

#### Blocks, inodes and directories

The file system divides the device into blocks (4096 bytes on ext4 by default). Four kinds of structure account for almost everything:

- The **superblock** records global parameters: block size, block count, inode count, feature flags and the state of the file system (clean or needing recovery).
- **Bitmaps** record which blocks and which inodes are free.
- The **inode table** holds one fixed-size inode per file object (256 bytes on the test image). An inode records type, mode, owner, size, timestamps, link count and the location of the data blocks. It does not record the file name.
- **Data blocks** hold file contents, directory contents and the journal.

A directory is a file whose contents are a list of entries, each pairing a name with an inode number. Names therefore live in directories, and one inode can have several names. The number of names is the link count of the inode; the inode and its blocks are released only when the link count and the count of open descriptors both reach zero.

#### The ext4 layout

ext4 divides large devices into block groups, each with its own bitmaps and inode table, so that an inode and its data stay physically close. The test image of 32 MiB had a single group. The values in the next figure are the real output of `dumpe2fs` and `debugfs` for that image.

blocks.text: An ext4 inode locates its data through an extent tree. An extent is a triple of logical block, length and physical block, so a contiguous file needs one entry, and up to four extents fit in the inode itself. Older ext2 and ext3 used block pointers, which were slower for large files. The extent of `app.log` in the experiment was a single entry: logical block 0, length 1, physical block 1551.

blocks.text:
#### Hard links, symbolic links and special inodes

A hard link is a second directory entry for the same inode. Both names are equal; there is no original. A symbolic link is a separate inode of type link whose content is a path string that is resolved at each access. Hard links cannot cross file systems (inode numbers are only unique within one file system) and cannot point to directories; symbolic links can do both, and they may dangle if the target is removed.

blocks.text:
Several inode numbers are reserved. Inode 2 is the root directory, inode 8 is the journal and inode 11 is `lost+found`, the directory in which recovery places orphaned files. In the experiment, `lost+found` was inode 11, `/var` inode 12, `/var/log` inode 13 and `app.log` inode 14, the first free numbers in order of creation.

#### Sparse files

A file may have a size larger than the blocks allocated to it. Unwritten regions read as zeros and occupy no blocks. In the experiment a 1 GiB file with one byte written at offset 512 MiB occupied 8 sectors of 512 bytes, that is one 4 KiB block:

blocks.code:
$ truncate -s 1G sparse.bin
$ echo x | dd of=sparse.bin bs=1 seek=536870912 conv=notrunc 2>/dev/null
$ ls -ls sparse.bin
4 -rw-r--r-- 1 root root 1073741824 Oct 18 02:20 sparse.bin
$ du -h sparse.bin; du -h --apparent-size sparse.bin
4.0K    sparse.bin
1.0G    sparse.bin
$ stat -c 'size=%s blocks=%b blocksize=%B' sparse.bin
size=1073741824 blocks=8 blocksize=512
blocks.title: A sparse file: apparent size 1 GiB, allocated 4 KiB

blocks.text:
The distinction explains differences between `ls -l` and `du`, and why copying a sparse file with a naive tool can fill a disk. Database files, virtual machine images and some core dumps are commonly sparse.

#### The VFS layer and the file system types

Applications call the same system calls regardless of the file system. The kernel dispatches them through the Virtual File System (VFS), which defines four object types that every file system implements or emulates: the superblock (one mounted instance), the inode, the dentry (a cached name-to-inode mapping) and the file (an open file description). The dentry cache is what makes repeated path lookups cheap.

blocks.text:
On the build machine `/proc/filesystems` listed ext2, ext3, ext4, xfs, overlay, tmpfs, squashfs, fuse and erofs among others, and the root file system was ext4 mounted on `/dev/vda` with options `rw,relatime,discard`.

#### Journaling and crash consistency

Creating a file changes several structures: the inode bitmap, the inode, the directory block and possibly the block bitmap. A power failure after some of these writes but before others leaves the file system inconsistent. Before journaling, the remedy was a full `fsck` scan at boot, which took hours on large disks. A journaling file system first writes a description of the planned metadata changes to a sequential log (the journal), marks the transaction complete with a commit record and only then writes the blocks to their home locations. After a crash, recovery replays committed transactions and discards incomplete ones in seconds.

ext4 offers three data modes, selected by the mount option `data=`:

- `data=ordered` (default): only metadata is journaled, but file data blocks are written to disk before the metadata that refers to them is committed. After a crash a file never exposes stale content from a previously deleted file, though recent appends may be missing.
- `data=writeback`: metadata is journaled and data is written in any order; faster, but a crash can expose old data inside a file whose size was updated.
- `data=journal`: data and metadata are both journaled; every block is written twice, which doubles write traffic but gives the strongest guarantee.

The kernel accepted all three modes on test images. After remounting with `data=journal`, `/proc/mounts` reported `rw,relatime,nodioread_nolock,nodelalloc,data=journal`, showing that the mode also disables delayed allocation; the writeback mode appeared as `data=writeback`.

blocks.text:
The journal protects the structure of the file system, not the application data. Metadata consistency after a crash does not mean that a multi-step application update is atomic. Applications that need atomicity use `fsync` at the right points, write-ahead logs or the atomic `rename` of a fully written temporary file; the next chapters return to this point.

#### Mounting and /etc/fstab

A file system becomes visible when it is attached to a directory with `mount`. The mount table is a tree: after the mount, the directory shows the root of the mounted file system, and the inode numbering restarts there. `/proc/mounts` and `findmnt` display the live table. The file `/etc/fstab` lists persistent mounts with device, mount point, type, options and the dump and fsck pass numbers. On the build machine `/etc/fstab` was an unconfigured placeholder because the machine was a minimal virtual environment; on a normal server it also names options such as `noatime` (avoid a metadata write on each read), `nofail` and `x-systemd.device-timeout`, whose absence is a cause of boot failures when a data disk is missing.

### Worked trace: resolving /var/log/app.log

The kernel resolves a path one component at a time, starting at the root dentry for an absolute path and at the current directory for a relative one. For every directory it checks that the caller has execute permission, looks up the next name in the directory contents and loads the inode. The trace below used the real structures of a 32 MiB test image; `debugfs` supplied the numbers.

blocks.caption: Eight lookups resolve the path: four reads of inodes (2, 12, 13, 14) interleaved with four reads of directory or data blocks, with an execute-permission check at each directory.
blocks.alt: open("/var/log/app.log") then read(): each box is one lookup (cached in the dentry and inode caches after the first) | 1 root inode 2 inode 2 -> extent: block 6 x ok? | 2 read block 6 entry "var" -> inode 12 | 3 inode 12 (/var) extent: block 1549 x ok? | 4 read block 1549 entry "log" -> inode 13 | 5 inode 13 (/var/log) extent: block 1550 x ok? | 6 read block 1550 entry "app.log" -> inode 14 | 7 inode 14 mode 0644, size 12, extent: block 1551 | 8 read block 1551 "hello inode"

blocks.text:
1. The kernel starts at the root inode, number 2. Its extent shows the directory contents at block 6. The root directory block lists `.`, `..`, `lost+found` (inode 11) and `var` (inode 12).
2. Inode 12 is located in the inode table. Group 0 has its inode table at block 37 and the inode size is 256 bytes, so inode 12 is at byte offset `(12 - 1) x 256 = 2816` within the table. Its mode is `0755` directory, so execute permission is checked for the caller. Its extent points to block 1549.
3. The block 1549 holds the entries of `/var`. A raw dump (`debugfs -R "bd 1549"`) shows the entry `log` with inode number 13, in little-endian bytes `0d 00 00 00`, a record length of `0x0fdc` and the name length 3.
4. Inode 13 (`/var/log`) is read; its directory block is 1550 and it holds `app.log` with inode 14.
5. Inode 14 is at block 37, byte offset `0x0d00 = 13 x 256`. Mode `0644`, size 12 and one extent at block 1551. The file name lookup is complete and the kernel allocates an open file description and a descriptor.
6. `read` then fetches block 1551 through the page cache and returns the 12 bytes `hello inode`.

On a running system, almost all of these reads are served from the dentry cache and inode cache in memory; the disk is touched only on a cold path. The cost of deep paths is therefore dominated by cache misses, not by the number of components.

### Hands-on

#### Building and inspecting a file system without a spare disk

A regular file can serve as a block device through the loop driver, which makes real file systems available for experiments without touching any production disk. The sequence below creates, mounts and inspects an ext4 image. The commands require root; paths are shortened.

blocks.code:
$ truncate -s 32M img.ext4 && mkfs.ext4 -q -F -L osw img.ext4
$ mount -o loop img.ext4 /mnt/t
$ dumpe2fs -h img.ext4 | grep -E "features|Inode count|Block count|Block size|Inode size|Journal"
Filesystem features:      has_journal ext_attr resize_inode dir_index filetype needs_recovery
                          extent
                          64bit flex_bg sparse_super large_file huge_file dir_nlink
                          extra_isize metadata_csum
Inode count:              8192
Block count:              8192
Block size:               4096
Inode size:               256
Journal inode:            8
Journal features:         journal_64bit journal_checksum_v3
$ dumpe2fs img.ext4 | sed -n '/^Group 0/,$p' | head -8
Group 0: (Blocks 0-8191) csum 0x4d71 [ITABLE_ZEROED]
  Primary superblock at 0, Group descriptors at 1-1

blocks.title: Create an ext4 image, mount it and read the block group layout

blocks.text:
The feature list contains `needs_recovery` because the image was inspected while mounted with a journal that had not been checkpointed. The journal itself is inode 8, a 4 MiB file whose extents were `(0-9):11-20, (10-24):22-36,` `(25-1023):550-1548`, which shows that a file system places its own metadata files in the gaps between the fixed structures.

#### Hard and symbolic links

$ ln var/log/app.log hard.log && ln -s var/log/app.log soft.log
$ ls -li . var/log

blocks.title: Two names, one inode; one name that stores a path

blocks.text:
`hard.log` and `app.log` share inode 14 with a link count of 2. The symbolic link is inode 15 with size 15, the length of the stored text `var/log/app.log`. Note that `Blocks: 8` counts 512-byte units: the 12-byte file occupies one 4096-byte block.

#### An overlay file system

Container images use overlayfs. The experiment mounts a lower directory with two files, adds an empty upper directory and a work directory, then modifies the merged view.

blocks.code:
$ mount -t overlay overlay -o lowerdir=ov/lower,upperdir=ov/upper,workdir=ov/work ov/merged
$ echo "changed" >> ov/merged/a.txt; rm ov/merged/b.txt; echo new > ov/merged/c.txt
$ ls -l ov/upper ov/merged
ov/merged:
total 8
-rw-r--r-- 1 root root 19 Oct 18 02:14 a.txt
-rw-r--r-- 1 root root  4 Oct 18 02:14 c.txt

ov/upper:
total 8
-rw-r--r-- 1 root root   19 Oct 18 02:14 a.txt
c--------- 2 root root 0, 0 Oct 18 02:14 b.txt
-rw-r--r-- 1 root root    4 Oct 18 02:14 c.txt
$ cat ov/lower/a.txt
from lower
$ stat -c '%n %F %t:%T' ov/upper/b.txt
ov/upper/b.txt character special file 0:0
blocks.title: Copy-up and whiteout in overlayfs

blocks.text: The first write to `a.txt` copied the entire file into the upper layer (the copy-up) and appended there, leaving the lower file untouched. The removal of `b.txt` created a whiteout, a character device with device number 0:0, which hides the lower file. Two consequences matter for operations. Writing a few bytes to a large file in an image copies the whole file on first write, which causes latency spikes for log files or databases placed in the container layer. Deleting a file that came from the image never frees space, so large data and logs belong on a volume, not in the writable layer.

blocks.text: #### Reading the journal

blocks.code:
$ debugfs -R "logdump" img4.ext4
Journal starts at block 1, transaction 2
Found expected sequence 2, type 1 (descriptor block) at block 1
Found expected sequence 2, type 2 (commit block) at block 10
No magic number at block 11: end of journal.
blocks.title: The journal of a freshly written image (typical)

blocks.text:
A transaction of sequence 2 consists of a descriptor block at journal block 1, the metadata blocks that follow it and a commit block at block 10. If the commit block had not reached the disk before a crash, replay would ignore the whole transaction. The journal size of 4 MiB (1024 blocks) bounds how much unwritten metadata can be pending.

### Real-world incidents

#### Incident: No space left on device with free blocks (inode exhaustion)

**Scenario.** A batch component of an order platform writes one small marker file per processed event into a directory on an ext4 volume. After several weeks the writes begin to fail although monitoring shows the volume at 4 percent block usage.

**Symptoms.** Java throws `java.io.IOException: No space left on device` from `File.createNewFile`, and shell commands such as `touch` fail with the same message. `df -h` shows ample free space. Writes to existing files still succeed.

**Diagnosis.** When `df -h` disagrees with the error, the next command is `df -i`, which reports inode usage. The reproduction used an image formatted with only 256 inodes so that the condition appears within seconds.

blocks.code:
$ mkfs.ext4 -q -N 256 -F img1.ext4 && mount -o loop img1.ext4 /mnt/t
$ df -h /mnt/t; df -i /mnt/t
Filesystem      Size  Used Avail Use% Mounted on
/dev/loop0       12M   24K   11M   1% /mnt/t
Filesystem     Inodes IUsed IFree IUse% Mounted on
/dev/loop0        256    11   245    5% /mnt/t
$ cd /mnt/t && mkdir t && cd t && for i in $(seq 1 300); do : > f$i || break; done
bash: f245: No space left on device
$ cd ..; df -h .; df -i .
Filesystem      Size  Used Avail Use% Mounted on
/dev/loop0       12M   28K   11M   1% /mnt/t
Filesystem     Inodes IUsed IFree IUse% Mounted on
/dev/loop0        256   256     0  100% /mnt/t
$ touch x
touch: cannot touch 'x': No space left on device
blocks.title: Reproduction on a 16 MiB ext4 image with 256 inodes

blocks.text: The block usage remained at 1 percent while inode usage reached 100 percent. The file system had 11 inodes in use at creation (the reserved inodes and `lost+found`) and refused the 245th new file.

blocks.text:
On a production volume the directory containing the millions of files is found with `find /data -xdev -type f -printf` `'%h\n' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head`, which counts files per directory. The `-xdev` option prevents the search from crossing into other mounts.

**write fails: No space left on device**

df -h /path : compare Use% with du -sx /path

Use% near 100, du agrees: du -xh Use% near 100, du far smaller than Used: space Use% low, blocks free: run df -i and check --max-depth=3 /path, find the largest held by files no name points to IUse% = 100 ? directories

Real files filled it: log flood, core dumps, temp lsof +L1: deleted but open files -\> restart, or Inode exhaustion: find / -xdev -type f files -\> rotate, cap, delete truncate via /proc/PID/fd/N awk dir counts -\> remove tiny files

Also check: reserved blocks for root (tune2fs -m), project/user quotas, a read-only remount after errors (mount shows ro), container writable layer limits, tmpfs size= limits, and Kubernetes ephemeral-storage limits

*Figure 5.17. The same error message has four causes;* `df -h`*,* `du`*,* `df -i` *and* `lsof +L1` *separate them in four commands.*

**Root cause.** ext4 fixes the number of inodes when the file system is created (by default one per 16 KiB of capacity), so a workload with many tiny files exhausts inodes long before blocks. The error code `ENOSPC` is shared by both conditions.

**Fix.** Immediate: delete or archive the small files (removing a directory with millions of entries is faster with `find dir` `-type f -delete` than with shell expansion, which fails with `Argument list too long`). Permanent: change the design so that events are written to one append-only file, to a database or to an object store; or recreate the file system with more inodes (`mkfs.ext4 -i 4096`) or use xfs, which allocates inodes dynamically.

**Prevention.** Alert on `node_filesystem_files_free` (or `df -i`) next to the block alert, with the same thresholds. Never use the file system as a key-value store with one file per key at scale.

#### Incident: hung process on a stale NFS mount

**Scenario.** A report generator reads input files from an NFS share mounted at `/mnt/share`. The storage server is restarted for maintenance and does not return for twenty minutes. **Symptoms.** The service stops responding. Thread dumps show request threads inside `FileInputStream.readBytes` or `File.exists`. `kill -15` has no effect, the pod does not terminate gracefully and the load average rises while CPU usage stays near zero. Even `ls /mnt/share` hangs in the terminal.

**Diagnosis.** The decisive observation is the process state. Processes waiting for an NFS reply are in uninterruptible sleep, shown as `D`. The output below is typical for this failure; it was not reproduced because no NFS server exists on the build machine.

blocks.code:
$ ps -eo pid,stat,wchan:32,cmd | awk '$2 ~ /^D/'
 2210 D    nfs_wait_on_request   java -jar app.jar
 2305 D    rpc_wait_bit_killable ls /mnt/share
$ dmesg | tail -2
nfs: server nas01 not responding, still trying
nfs: server nas01 not responding, still trying
$ grep nfs /proc/mounts
nas01:/export/reports /mnt/share nfs4 rw,relatime,vers=4.2,hard,timeo=600,retrans=2 0 0
blocks.title: Typical diagnosis of a hard NFS mount that is not responding

blocks.text: The `D` state, the `wchan` function names and the kernel message together identify the file system as the blocked layer. Tools that touch the mount, such as `df` and `lsof`, hang too; `df -l` (local file systems only) and `mount` are safe.

blocks.text:
**Root cause.** With the default `hard` option the NFS client retries a request forever so as not to lose data, and the blocked task cannot be interrupted by ordinary signals. The service placed network file access on its request path without a timeout.

**Fix.** Immediate: restore the server or its network path; blocked tasks then continue. If the server cannot return, `umount` `-f /mnt/share` aborts pending requests, and `umount -l` detaches the mount from the tree lazily. Permanent: keep request-path I/O off network file systems; perform the access in a bounded executor with a timeout so that a hang consumes one worker, not all threads; use `soft` with explicit `timeo` and `retrans` only for data that tolerates failure, because a soft mount can return `EIO` in the middle of a write and corrupt output.

**Prevention.** Alert on the count of processes in state `D` and on a load average that rises while CPU is idle. Mount shares with a health check, and make the readiness probe verify the dependency with a timeout rather than a plain `stat`.

### Questions to expect

#### What does an inode contain, and what does it not contain?

It contains the file type, mode, owner, size, timestamps, link count and the locations of the data blocks (extents on ext4). It does not contain the file name; names are entries in directories that map a name to an inode number.

#### What is the difference between a hard link and a symbolic link?

A hard link is another directory entry for the same inode, indistinguishable from the original and valid only within one file system. A symbolic link is a separate inode containing a path that is resolved at access time; it may cross file systems and may dangle.

#### Why does deleting a large log file sometimes not free disk space?

Deletion removes the name and decrements the link count. The inode and blocks remain while any process holds the file open, so space is freed only when the last descriptor closes. `lsof +L1` lists such files.

#### How can a file system have free blocks and still return ENOSPC?

It may have run out of inodes (`df -i`), reached a quota or the reserved-block threshold, or the file may live on a small tmpfs or overlay. Inode exhaustion arises with very many small files.

#### What problem does journaling solve, and what does it not solve?

It keeps file system metadata consistent after a crash by replaying committed transactions, which avoids a full `fsck`. It does not make application updates atomic and, in the default ordered mode, does not guarantee that recently written data survives without `fsync`.

#### Describe the steps the kernel takes to open /var/log/app.log.

It starts at the root inode, checks execute permission on each directory, looks up the next name in the directory contents (using the dentry cache when possible), loads the inode and repeats until the final component, then allocates an open file description and a descriptor. Each directory lookup reads at most one inode and one directory block on a cold cache.

#### How does overlayfs support container images?

It presents a union of read-only lower layers and a writable upper layer. A first write copies the file into the upper layer, deletions are recorded as whiteouts and lower layers stay unchanged, so many containers share one image. Heavy writes belong on volumes because of the copy-up cost.

#### What is a sparse file?

A file whose size exceeds its allocated blocks because unwritten ranges are holes that read as zeros. `ls -l` shows the apparent size, `du` the allocated size.

#### What is the effect of a hard NFS mount when the server disappears?

Requests are retried indefinitely; threads touching the mount enter uninterruptible sleep and cannot be terminated by ordinary signals until the server returns or the mount is forced off.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
Key points

- A file system maps names to inodes (directories), inodes to blocks (extents) and tracks free space in bitmaps; the inode count is fixed at creation on ext4.
- Path resolution is a sequence of directory lookups with permission checks; caches make it cheap, and the real cost is on a cold path.
- Hard links share an inode; the data is freed only when the link count and the open count reach zero, which explains deleted-but-open files.
- The journal protects metadata consistency; durability of application data still requires `fsync`, and ordered mode writes data before the metadata that refers to it.
- `df -h`, `df -i`, `du` and `lsof +L1` separate the four causes of ENOSPC; overlayfs copy-up and whiteouts explain container storage behaviour.

sections.title: Storage Devices and the Block Layer

blocks.text:
A file system decides which blocks to read or write; the block layer and the device decide how fast that happens. The latency of a storage device is three to five orders of magnitude above that of memory, and the difference between a service that answers in 5 milliseconds and one that answers in 500 is frequently a queue in front of a disk. This chapter describes the device classes, the kernel path to them, the aggregation layers (RAID and LVM) and the counters that measure utilisation, so that a statement such as "the disk is the bottleneck" can be proved or refuted from `/proc/diskstats` with arithmetic.

### Concept and mechanism

#### Hard disks and solid-state devices

A hard disk drive (HDD) reads and writes through a head that moves over spinning platters. A random access pays a seek (moving the head, typically a few to ten milliseconds) and a rotational delay (on average half a revolution: 4.17 ms at 7200 rpm). A sequential access pays these costs once and then streams at the platter speed. An HDD therefore delivers on the order of one hundred random operations per second but a hundred or more megabytes per second sequentially. The kernel and databases are designed to turn random access into sequential access wherever possible: merging adjacent requests, ordering by address, appending to logs.

A solid-state drive (SSD) stores data in flash memory without moving parts. Reads of a page take tens of microseconds and many chips work in parallel, so random reads are almost as fast as sequential reads and tens of thousands of operations per second are normal. Flash has two constraints that shape its behaviour. A page cannot be overwritten in place: it must be erased as part of a much larger erase block, so the controller remaps logical blocks to fresh pages (the flash translation layer) and later reclaims stale pages by garbage collection. The extra writes this causes are called write amplification, and the pauses it causes appear as latency spikes under sustained random writes. The `discard` (TRIM) command tells the device which blocks the file system no longer uses, so that reclamation is cheaper; the root file system of the build machine was mounted with `discard`.

blocks.text:
NVMe devices attach to the PCIe bus and support many hardware queues (up to 65535 queues of up to 65536 entries in the specification), so several CPUs can submit requests without sharing a lock. A SATA disk exposes one queue of 32 commands. A virtual machine disk (virtio-blk) is a software queue whose speed is set by the hypervisor and the backing storage; cloud volumes add network latency and a provisioned operations-per-second budget that the volume enforces by throttling.

#### The path through the kernel

A `write` to a file reaches the block layer only after the page cache and the file system. The block layer turns file system requests into `bio` structures (a list of memory pages and a target sector range), merges adjacent bios into larger requests, places them into queues and hands them to the driver. The I/O scheduler decides the order within a queue. The available schedulers are visible per device in `/sys/block/DEV/queue/scheduler`; the active one is in brackets.

blocks.title: Block device parameters (build machine, typical for a virtio disk)

blocks.text:
Three entries need interpretation. `rotational` is 1 although the disk is virtual: the flag is a default of the virtio driver and must not be used to decide whether a disk is an SSD. `write_cache` set to `write back` means that the device has a volatile cache, so the kernel must send explicit flush commands to make data durable; that cost appears in the measurement of `fsync` in the next chapter. `read_ahead_kb` of 128 means that after sequential reads the kernel prefetches up to 128 KiB.

#### Queue depth and parallelism

The queue depth is the number of requests outstanding at the device. A depth of one serialises operations and wastes the parallelism of an SSD; a very deep queue raises throughput but also raises latency, because a newly submitted request waits behind everything already queued. The relation is Little's law: the average number of requests in the system equals the arrival rate multiplied by the average time each spends in the system. A device that sustains 200 writes per second with a mean latency of 38 ms must have on average 7.6 requests in flight, which matches the measurement below.

#### RAID and LVM

Redundant arrays of independent disks combine several devices for capacity, speed and failure tolerance. A hardware RAID controller presents the array as one disk, often with a battery-backed write cache; software RAID (`md`) and file systems such as ZFS and btrfs implement the same ideas in the kernel.

blocks.text:
RAID is availability, not backup: a deletion, a corruption or an application bug is replicated to every copy immediately. For database volumes in the cloud the relevant redundancy is usually provided by the storage service, and the guest only sees one device.

The Logical Volume Manager (LVM) inserts a layer between disks and file systems. Physical volumes are pooled into a volume group, from which logical volumes of arbitrary size are carved. A logical volume can be extended while mounted and followed by `resize2fs` (ext4) or `xfs_growfs` (xfs, which cannot shrink). Snapshots use copy-on-write extents and are the basis of consistent backups.

blocks.text:
### Worked trace: utilisation and latency from /proc/diskstats

Every block device has one line in `/proc/diskstats` (and a shorter one in `/sys/block/DEV/stat`). The fields, after the major number, minor number and device name, are cumulative counters since boot. The tools `iostat` and `sar` merely subtract two samples; they were not installed on the build machine, so the calculation was done by hand, which is also the clearest way to learn the meaning of each field.

rows: summed over all requests, so it can exceed wall time
wall time during which at least one request was in flight
requests in flight multiplied by time, accumulated

blocks.text:
*The fields used in the calculation (kernel 6.x documentation, Documentation/admin-guide/iostats).*

The workload was `dd if=/dev/zero of=big bs=1M count=150 conv=fdatasync`, which writes 150 MiB and flushes it once. The counters of `vda` were captured immediately before and after; the elapsed time measured by the shell was 214.8 ms.

blocks.title: Before and after samples (the fields of interest, from the build machine)

blocks.caption: Subtracting the two samples and dividing by the interval gives utilisation 55.9 percent, write latency 38.0 ms, an average queue of 7.8 requests and 732 MB/s.
blocks.alt: /proc/diskstats for vda around dd bs=1M count=150 conv=fdatasync (interval 214.8 ms) | field meaning before after delta | 5 writes completed 5041 5083 42 | 7 sectors written (512 B) 76640 383880 307240 | 8 ms spent writing 1557 3153 1596 | 10 ms doing I/O (busy) 4352 4472 120 | 11 weighted ms (queue x time) 14716 16394 1678 | utilisation 120 ms busy / 214.8 ms = 55.9 % | write await 1596 ms / 42 writes = 38.0 ms per write | average queue size 1678 ms / 214.8 ms = 7.8 requests | average write size 307240 x 512 B / 42 = 3658 KiB | throughput 307240 x 512 B / 0.2148 s = 732 MB/s | Utilisation near 100 % means saturated only for a single-queue device; SSDs serve many requests in parallel.

blocks.text:
1. Write requests completed: 5083 - 5041 = 42, which is 42 / 0.2148 s = 195.5 write operations per second.
2. Sectors written: 383880 - 76640 = 307240, which is 307240 x 512 B = 157.3 MB; divided by 0.2148 s the throughput is 732 MB/s. The average request therefore carried 307240 x 512 / 42 = 3.66 MB, far above the 128 KiB readahead size, because the block layer merged adjacent pages into large requests.
3. Time spent writing: 3153 - 1557 = 1596 ms summed over all requests; divided by 42 requests this is a mean latency (`await`) of 38.0 ms. The value includes the time in the queue and the time at the device. Because the requests were large and queued behind each other, a large latency here is expected and does not indicate a slow device.
4. Busy time: 4472 - 4352 = 120 ms during the 214.8 ms interval gives a utilisation of 55.9 percent. The field counts time with at least one request outstanding; it does not say how much more the device could have done.
5. Weighted time: 16394 - 14716 = 1678 ms; divided by the interval this is an average queue size of 7.81. Little's law check: 195.5 operations per second x 0.038 s = 7.4 requests in flight, with the remainder explained by the two reads and the flush.
6. The last two fields are flush counters: one flush request completed (1248 to 1249) and consumed 81 ms (124 to 205). That single cache flush, issued by `fdatasync`, accounts for 38 percent of the elapsed time.

The calculation illustrates why `%util` is misleading for devices that handle many requests in parallel: an NVMe drive can be at 100 percent utilisation (always at least one request in flight) while delivering a small part of its capacity. For such devices the queue size and the latency are more informative than utilisation.

### Hands-on

#### Sampling a device over time

A short shell function turns the counters into rates; it is shown for the write side. The read side uses the neighbouring fields (indices 3, 5 and 6 of the array).

blocks.code:
#!/bin/bash
# usage: diskrate.sh DEVICE SECONDS
dev=$1; sec=$2
read -r -a a < <(awk -v d="$dev" '$3==d' /proc/diskstats)
sleep "$sec"
read -r -a b < <(awk -v d="$dev" '$3==d' /proc/diskstats)
# index: 7=writes completed, 9=sectors written, 10=ms writing, 12=ms doing I/O, 13=weighted
w=$(( b[7] - a[7] )); sw=$(( b[9] - a[9] )); mw=$(( b[10] - a[10] ))
busy=$(( b[12] - a[12] )); wt=$(( b[13] - a[13] ))
awk -v w="$w" -v sw="$sw" -v mw="$mw" -v busy="$busy" -v wt="$wt" -v s="$sec" 'BEGIN {
  printf "w/s=%.1f  MB/s=%.1f  await=%.2f ms  util=%.1f%%  avgq=%.2f\n",
    w/s, sw*512/1e6/s, (w ? mw/w : 0), busy/(s*10), wt/(s*1000) }'
blocks.title: diskrate.sh

blocks.code:
$ ./diskrate.sh vda 3
w/s=7820.7  MB/s=181.6  await=0.07 ms  util=65.6%  avgq=0.99

blocks.text:
#### The device as a process sees it

Per-process counters are in `/proc/PID/io`: `rchar` and `wchar` count bytes passed through `read` and `write` (including cached data), whereas `read_bytes` and `write_bytes` count bytes that were actually submitted to the block layer. The difference between the two shows how much of the I/O of a process was absorbed by the page cache. The incident below uses these fields.

### Real-world incidents

#### Incident: high iowait and a slow service

**Scenario.** An order service in a Kubernetes pod writes a transaction journal to a persistent volume. After a release that reduced the batching of journal writes, request latency grows from 20 ms to over 300 ms during peak traffic. CPU graphs show moderate load.

**Symptoms.** The load average of the node is high compared with the CPU count while the `us` and `sy` columns of `vmstat` are low. Thread dumps show many threads in the journal-writing code, not in the database driver. **Diagnosis.** The first question is whether threads wait for the disk. The commands below were run against `FsyncLoop.java`, a Java program that appends 64 KiB and calls `force(true)` in a loop, which reproduces the I/O pattern of a journal with one flush per record.

blocks.title: FsyncLoop.java

blocks.title: Diagnosis during one 16-second run (build machine, typical; vmstat rows 1 to 4)

blocks.text:
The reading of the output follows the decision path of the figure. The `b` column of `vmstat` shows one blocked process and the `wa` column 22 to 35 percent, so CPUs were idle while a task waited for I/O. The pressure stall information confirms it: `some avg10=22.61` means that for 22 percent of the last ten seconds at least one task was stalled on I/O, and `full` at 19 percent means that all non-idle tasks were stalled. The state of the Java thread was `D` (uninterruptible sleep) in `submit_bio_wait`, the kernel function in which a task waits for a block request to complete. The per-process counters show 1.8 GB written by 27475 write calls, with `write_bytes` equal to `wchar`: nothing was absorbed by the page cache because every write was forced.

The device counters give the decisive nuance. The disk was 65.6 percent busy, yet `await` was only 0.07 ms and the average queue 0.99: the device was not slow and not queued, it was kept busy by a stream of strictly serial tiny requests (a data write, a journal write and a flush per commit), 7820 per second. The thread, not the device, was the limit: 41651 commits in 16 s is one commit every 0.38 ms. Adding bandwidth would not help; fewer and larger commits would. An earlier run of the same program, made while other processes kept both CPUs of the shared build machine busy, showed `wa` of only 0 to 13 percent and `b` of 0 although the thread was in `D` state. The reason is that `iowait` is counted only while a CPU is idle, so a busy machine hides blocked threads. The `D` state and the pressure values were reliable in both runs and are the primary indicators.

blocks.text:
**Root cause.** The release replaced batched journal writes with one `force(true)` per record. Each record paid a full device round trip including a cache flush, and the volume had a limited number of operations per second, so threads queued behind the device.

**Fix.** Immediate: raise the batch size or the commit interval so that many records share one flush (group commit); move the journal to a faster or dedicated volume; scale out the number of volumes. Permanent: acknowledge records only after a group flush, with a bounded delay such as a few milliseconds, instead of one flush per record. Measure the achieved operations per second against the provisioned limit of the volume.

**Prevention.** Alert on pressure stall `io some avg10` above 10 percent, on the await of the data volume and on the proximity to the provisioned I/O budget. Include the commit mode in load tests: a test that writes to a RAM disk (tmpfs) cannot reveal flush costs, as the measurement in the next chapter shows.

### Questions to expect

**Why is random I/O slower than sequential I/O on an HDD, and does the same hold for an SSD?** On an HDD each random access needs a head seek and a rotational delay of several milliseconds, whereas sequential access pays them once. An SSD has no mechanical delay, so random reads are close to sequential speed; random writes still suffer from erase-block management and write amplification.

#### What does the I/O scheduler do, and is it needed on NVMe?

It orders and merges requests within the block layer and prevents starvation (mq-deadline gives every request an expiry). NVMe devices have many hardware queues and internal scheduling, so `none` is commonly used.

#### What does `iowait` mean?

It is the share of time in which a CPU was idle while at least one task was waiting for I/O. It is not a measure of disk load: a busy CPU hides waiting tasks, and a CPU with nothing to do shows waiting that is harmless. Pressure stall information and per-device latency are more reliable.

#### How are utilisation and latency of a disk computed from `/proc/diskstats`?

Take two samples. Utilisation is the increase of the busy-time field divided by the wall time; latency is the increase of the time spent reading or writing divided by the number of completed requests; average queue size is the increase of the weighted time divided by the wall time.

#### Why can a device at 100 percent utilisation still have spare capacity?

The busy-time field counts time with at least one request outstanding. An SSD or NVMe device processes many requests in parallel, so it can be busy all the time while serving only a fraction of its throughput.

#### What are the trade-offs between RAID 1, RAID 5 and RAID 10?

RAID 1 mirrors (half capacity, fast reads, tolerates one failure per pair). RAID 5 stripes with parity (capacity of N-1 disks, tolerates one failure, slow small writes because of the read-modify-write of parity). RAID 10 stripes over mirrors (half capacity, good read and write performance, tolerates one failure per mirror pair). None of them replaces backup.

#### What is the purpose of LVM?

It separates logical volumes from physical disks so that volumes can be resized online, spread over several disks and snapshotted. The file system on top must be grown separately.

#### What is write amplification?

The ratio of data physically written to flash to the data written by the host, caused by erase-block granularity and garbage collection. High amplification reduces speed and lifetime of the device.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
Key points

- Device latency exceeds memory latency by orders of magnitude; the kernel hides it with the page cache, merging, read-ahead and queues, each of which adds its own latency under load.
- The counters of `/proc/diskstats` yield rate, latency, queue size and utilisation by simple subtraction; Little's law checks the result.
- `%util` is not capacity for parallel devices, and `iowait` is hidden by busy CPUs; pressure stall information, `D`-state threads and per-device await are better indicators.
- A device with a volatile write cache needs explicit flushes for durability; RAID 5 penalises small writes and no RAID level is a backup.
- Reduce the number of synchronous commits (group commit) before buying faster storage.

sections.title: Buffered I/O, the Page Cache and Durability

blocks.text:
A call to `write` returns in a few microseconds although a disk needs milliseconds. The difference is the page cache: the kernel copies the data into memory, marks the pages dirty and writes them out later. This design makes ordinary file I/O fast, but it also means that a successful `write` does not imply that the data is stored safely. Databases, message brokers and any service that promises to retain accepted data must therefore control when data reaches stable media. This chapter explains the write path, the system calls that control durability, their measured cost and the window of loss that remains when they are omitted.

### Concept and mechanism

#### The write path

The sequence of a buffered write is as follows. The application passes a buffer to `write` (for Java, `FileOutputStream.write` or `FileChannel.write`, which end in the same system call; `BufferedOutputStream` merely reduces the number of calls). The kernel copies the bytes into pages of the page cache that belong to the file, marks those pages dirty and returns. At a later time kernel writeback threads select dirty pages, ask the file system to map them to disk blocks and submit them through the block layer. The device may hold the data in its own volatile cache before it reaches stable media.

blocks.text:
Reads use the same cache. A `read` first looks up the page; a hit is a memory copy, a miss submits a block request and blocks the thread. The kernel also detects sequential access and prefetches ahead of the reader. Pages of the cache that are clean can be dropped at any time when memory is needed, so the cache grows to use free memory without harming applications; the accounting of this memory in `free` is treated in the Part on memory management.

#### Writeback policy

The kernel starts writing dirty data when any of three conditions is reached. These are controlled by sysctl parameters; the build machine reported the common defaults:

blocks.code:
$ sysctl vm.dirty_ratio vm.dirty_background_ratio \
    vm.dirty_expire_centisecs vm.dirty_writeback_centisecs
vm.dirty_ratio = 20
vm.dirty_background_ratio = 10
vm.dirty_expire_centisecs = 3000
vm.dirty_writeback_centisecs = 500
blocks.title: Writeback parameters (build machine)

blocks.text:
- Background writeback starts when dirty pages exceed `vm.dirty_background_ratio` percent of reclaimable memory (10 percent); the process continues to write without being delayed.
- When dirty pages exceed `vm.dirty_ratio` percent (20 percent), the writing process itself is throttled and forced to write, which appears as sudden latency in `write` calls.
- Regardless of volume, the writeback threads wake every `vm.dirty_writeback_centisecs` (5 seconds) and write pages that have been dirty longer than `vm.dirty_expire_centisecs` (30 seconds).

The implication is a bound on the age of unwritten data: a dirty page is written within roughly 30 to 35 seconds unless the process forces it earlier. That interval is the window in which a power failure loses data that the application believed to be written.

blocks.text:
A process that crashes does not lose cached writes, because the kernel owns the pages: only a failure of the kernel, the machine or the device loses them. Applications and operators often confuse the two kinds of failure when they reason about durability.

#### The durability system calls

as `fsync`, but skips metadata not needed to read the data (for example the modification time)
every `write` behaves as if followed by `fsync`

blocks.caption: Calls and flags that control when data becomes durable.

blocks.text:
The mapping of the Java methods was verified with `strace`: a program calling `force(true)` produced `fsync(4)`, one calling `force(false)` produced `fdatasync(4)` (five calls each in the test run).

An `fsync` of a file does not make the directory entry of a newly created file durable. After creating a file, a program that needs the name to survive a crash must also `fsync` the containing directory; in Java this is `FileChannel.open(dir,` `READ).force(true)`, which works on Linux. The ordering rules of the journal give a common safe pattern for replacing a file atomically: write a temporary file in the same directory, `fsync` it, rename it over the target and `fsync` the directory.

#### The device cache and flush

Storage devices have volatile write caches. A completed block write means only that the device accepted the data. `fsync` therefore ends with a flush command (or issues writes with the force-unit-access flag) so that the device writes its cache to media. Enterprise devices with power-loss protection treat the flush as nearly free; consumer devices do not. A device or hypervisor that acknowledges flushes without honouring them breaks every durability guarantee above it, which is a documented cause of corrupted databases on misconfigured virtual disks. The build machine reported `write_cache` as `write back`, so flushes were required.

#### Why databases and brokers care

A relational database makes a transaction durable by appending its redo record to a write-ahead log and calling `fsync` before it reports the commit; the data pages are written lazily. PostgreSQL does this with `fsync` and `synchronous_commit` enabled by default, and MySQL InnoDB with `innodb_flush_log_at_trx_commit=1`. Relaxing the setting (to a one-second flush interval) multiplies throughput but accepts the loss of up to one second of committed transactions after a crash. Redis with `appendfsync everysec` has the same trade-off. Apache Kafka takes a different position: by default it does not call `fsync` per message (the flush interval properties default to unlimited) and relies on replication to several brokers for durability, leaving the page cache to write segments. A cluster in which all replicas lose power simultaneously can therefore lose acknowledged messages, whereas a single broker failure cannot.

A further subtlety is the failure of `fsync` itself. When a write to the device fails, Linux marks the affected pages clean and reports the error once; a repeated `fsync` of the same file may then return success although the data was never written. PostgreSQL treats an `fsync` failure as fatal for this reason since 2018, and applications that retry after an I/O error assume the data is safe at their peril.

### Worked trace: the life of one 4 KiB durable record

The following steps follow one record of a journal written by `FileChannel.write(buf)` followed by `force(true)`; the durations are the medians measured on the build machine (typical, from the experiment below).

1. The JVM calls `write(fd, buf, 4096)`. The kernel copies 4096 bytes into a page cache page and marks it dirty. About 7.5 microseconds elapse; the file size in the inode grows.
2. The JVM calls `fsync(fd)`. The file system starts a journal transaction: it writes the data block first (ordered mode), then the journal descriptor with the changed metadata (inode size and timestamps, block bitmap, extent).
3. The kernel writes the commit block with a flush so that all earlier journal blocks are on media before it. The commit block is only valid if everything before it is durable.
4. The device flush completes, the transaction is committed and `fsync` returns. About 214 microseconds per call elapsed in the measurement on the root disk and about 720 microseconds on the loop-mounted image (which adds a second file system layer).
5. Later, the checkpoint writes the metadata from the journal to its home location, outside the latency path of the application.

The cost of step 2 to 4 is thirty times that of step 1, and the next experiment measures it directly.

### Hands-on

#### Measuring the cost of synchronisation

The program writes 200 blocks of 4 KiB in three modes: without synchronisation, with `force(false)` and with `force(true)` after every write.

blocks.text:
Three observations follow. Forced writes on the root disk cost between 214 and 249 microseconds, about thirty times the cost of the buffered write. The `force(false)` run was not faster than `force(true)` because every write extends the file, so the size change is metadata that `fdatasync` must flush as well; the difference between the two calls appears only for overwrites of already allocated blocks. On tmpfs a synchronisation call costs nothing because there is no device behind it, so a test on a RAM disk reports an optimistic result for any durable workload. The numbers on a different disk, a cloud volume or with a different load will differ; the ratio is the lesson.
