blocks.alt: Measured cost per 4 KiB write (microseconds, log scale, build VM, typical) | Java write, page cache only 7.5 | Java force(true) each write 213.8 | Java force(false) each write 248.6 | dd bs=4k (buffered) 4.2 | dd conv=fdatasync (once at end) 13.4 | dd oflag=direct 87 | dd oflag=dsync (every write) 1684.3 | Java force(true) on tmpfs 5.9 | 1 10 100 1000 | Synchronous writes cost 30 to 400 times a page-cache write; group commit amortises the flush.

blocks.text:
The four runs differ by a factor of 400. `conv=fdatasync` flushes once at the end, so the 2000 writes share one flush. `oflag=direct` bypasses the page cache but is not durable by itself. `oflag=dsync` makes each of the 2000 writes wait for the device, 1.68 ms per write. The conclusion for design is that the number of flushes, not the number of bytes, dominates durable throughput, which is the reason for group commit: collect the records of many concurrent requests into one write and one flush.

#### Dirty pages become visible

blocks.code:
$ dd if=/dev/zero of=t2.bin bs=1M count=64
67108864 bytes (67 MB, 64 MiB) copied, 0.0305604 s, 2.2 GB/s
$ grep -E "^(Dirty|Writeback):" /proc/meminfo
Dirty:             67000 kB
Writeback:             0 kB
$ sync; grep -E "^(Dirty|Writeback):" /proc/meminfo
Dirty:                72 kB
Writeback:             0 kB
blocks.title: Dirty memory after a buffered write of 64 MiB (build machine, typical)

blocks.text:
The `dd` command reported 2.2 GB/s because it measured only the copy into memory. At the moment it finished, 67000 kB were dirty and nothing was written yet; `sync` forced the write and returned the counters to near zero. Monitoring the `Dirty` and `Writeback` fields shows whether the system is accumulating unwritten data.

#### The read side

blocks.code:
$ dd if=r.bin of=/dev/null bs=1M
134217728 bytes (134 MB, 128 MiB) copied, 0.0181431 s, 7.4 GB/s
$ dd if=r.bin of=/dev/null bs=1M iflag=direct
134217728 bytes (134 MB, 128 MiB) copied, 0.0563702 s, 2.4 GB/s
$ dd if=r.bin iflag=nocache count=0           # evict this file from the cache
$ dd if=r.bin of=/dev/null bs=1M              # cold read, fills the cache
134217728 bytes (134 MB, 128 MiB) copied, 0.0502132 s, 2.7 GB/s
$ dd if=r.bin of=/dev/null bs=1M              # warm read
134217728 bytes (134 MB, 128 MiB) copied, 0.0201377 s, 6.7 GB/s
blocks.title: Warm cache against direct reads of the same 128 MiB file (build machine, typical)

blocks.text:
The warm read was about 2.5 times faster than the cold read. The ratio on this machine is modest because the virtual disk is backed by the host cache; on a physical disk the difference is two to four orders of magnitude. System-wide eviction with `echo 3 > /proc/sys/vm/drop_caches` was not used because it affects every process on the machine and slows them all; it is acceptable for benchmarks on dedicated hosts and wrong as a production remedy.

#### Atomic file replacement

blocks.title: AtomicWrite.java

blocks.code:
$ java AtomicWrite.java /data/aw/app.conf
version=2
entry: app.conf
$ strace -f -e trace=fsync,rename -o aw.st java AtomicWrite.java /data/aw/app.conf
$ grep -E "fsync|rename" aw.st | head -6
fsync(6)                          = 0
rename("/data/aw/cfg17957079634848529826.tmp", "/data/aw/app.conf") = 0
fsync(6)                          = 0
fsync(6)                          = 0
rename("/data/aw/cfg4243081716996555018.tmp", "/data/aw/app.conf") = 0
fsync(6)                          = 0
blocks.title: Run and system call trace of the pattern

blocks.text:
The trace shows the required order: `fsync` of the temporary file, `rename`, `fsync` of the directory. Readers of the target file see either the old or the new content in full, and after a crash the same holds, because the rename is a metadata operation of a single journal transaction.

### Real-world incidents

#### Incident: intermittent latency spikes from slow fsync

**Scenario.** A payment service commits each transaction to an embedded write-ahead log with `fsync`. It shares the volume with a nightly batch job that exports data to large files. Median latency is 2 ms, but several times per night the 99th percentile jumps to seconds and the circuit breakers of upstream services open.

**Symptoms.** Latency graphs show spikes that coincide with the start of the export. CPU and heap are normal. Application logs show nothing, but a thread dump taken during a spike shows commit threads inside `FileChannel.force`.

**Diagnosis.** The aim is to show that the `fsync` latency of the service rises when a bulk writer shares the device, and to find the writer. The reproduction used `FsyncLatency.java`, which measures every `force(true)` of a 4 KiB write, once alone and once while a `dd` loop wrote 200 MB files with `fsync` on the same disk.

blocks.title: FsyncLatency.java

blocks.code:
$ java FsyncLatency.java /data/commit.log 8
n=2959  p50=0.49 ms  p99=1.25 ms  max=35.87 ms
$ (for i in 1 2 3 4; do dd if=/dev/zero of=/data/bulk.bin bs=1M count=200 conv=fsync; done) &
$ java FsyncLatency.java /data/commit.log 8
n=2588  p50=0.63 ms  p99=5.87 ms  max=81.05 ms
blocks.title: Commit latency alone and next to a bulk writer (build machine, shared VM, typical)

blocks.text: The median moved little (0.49 to 0.63 ms) while the 99th percentile grew by a factor of 4.7 and the maximum by a factor of 2.3. This is the signature of queueing behind bulk I/O: most commits find a short queue, a few find the queue full of large requests. On the shared test machine the effect is small; on a volume with a provisioned throughput budget, a 3 GB export can fill the queue for seconds. To find the culprit on a real host, the per-process counters `write_bytes` in `/proc/PID/io` are sampled twice and subtracted, and `ps -L` with `wchan` shows which threads wait for the device.

blocks.text:
**Root cause.** The write-ahead log and a bulk writer shared one device and one queue. A synchronous flush has to wait for the requests already queued, and the file system journal can also serialise the commit behind the dirty data of the large file.

**Fix.** Immediate: move or throttle the export (for example with `ionice -c3` (honoured by `bfq` and, in recent kernels, by `mq-deadline`), a cgroup `io.max` limit, or by writing in smaller chunks with an explicit pause). Permanent: place the write-ahead log on its own volume; limit the dirty memory a bulk writer can accumulate (`vm.dirty_background_bytes`, `vm.dirty_bytes`) so that writeback is continuous instead of bursty; use group commit to reduce the number of flushes.

**Prevention.** Track the 99th and 99.9th percentile of the commit duration as a metric of its own; alert on `fsync` duration, not only on request latency. Schedule batch work away from peak hours and give it a throttled, separate volume.

### Questions to expect

#### What is the difference between `write` and `fsync`?

`write` copies data into the page cache and returns; the data is lost if the machine fails before writeback. `fsync` blocks until the data and the metadata of the file are on stable storage, including a device cache flush.

#### What is the difference between `fsync` and `fdatasync`?

`fdatasync` flushes only the metadata that is required to retrieve the data (for example a new file size), skipping others such as the modification time, so it can avoid one journal write. For appends the difference is small because the size changes.

#### What does `O_DIRECT` do, and does it make writes durable?

It bypasses the page cache and transfers between user buffers and the device, with alignment requirements. It does not by itself guarantee durability because the device cache may still be volatile; it is combined with `O_DSYNC` or `fsync`. Databases use it to avoid double caching.

#### Why does a database call `fsync` on its log but not on its data files at commit?

The log is sequential, so one flush makes the transaction recoverable. The data pages can be written lazily because recovery re-applies the log to them. This turns many random writes into one sequential flush.

#### When is a process crash different from a power failure for written data?

After a process crash the kernel still owns the dirty pages and writes them, so data passed to `write` survives. A power failure or kernel panic loses everything not yet written to stable storage.

#### How is a file replaced atomically?

Write a temporary file in the same directory, `fsync` it, `rename` it over the target (atomic on one file system), then `fsync` the directory. Readers and crash recovery see the old or the new file, never a mixture.

#### What controls when dirty pages are written?

Background writeback starts at `vm.dirty_background_ratio`, writers are throttled at `vm.dirty_ratio`, and pages older than `vm.dirty_expire_centisecs` (30 s by default) are written by threads that wake every `vm.dirty_writeback_centisecs` (5 s).

#### Why can a benchmark on tmpfs mislead?

There is no device, so `fsync` costs nothing; the measurement hides the dominant cost of durable workloads.

#### How does Kafka obtain durability without calling `fsync` per message?

By replicating each partition to several brokers and acknowledging according to `acks` and `min.insync.replicas`; the operating system writes segments from the page cache. Simultaneous loss of all replicas can still lose data.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
Key points

- `write` copies into the page cache and returns; data is stable only after `fsync` or `fdatasync` has returned, which includes a device flush.
- Dirty pages are written within about 30 to 35 seconds by default; a process crash loses nothing, a power failure loses the unwritten window.
- Durable writes cost 30 to 400 times a cached write on the measured machine; the number of flushes dominates, so batch commits (group commit).
- A durable file replacement is temporary file, `fsync`, `rename`, `fsync` of the directory.
- Tests on tmpfs or with `fsync` disabled hide the cost and the risk; a bulk writer on the same device raises the tail latency of commits.

A network service must wait for data that arrives at moments it does not control, and it must wait for thousands of connections at once. The strategy for waiting determines how many threads a server needs, how much memory they consume and how the server behaves under load. The operating system offers five models, from the simplest blocking call to asynchronous submission, and every Java server framework is a choice among them. This chapter defines the models by the moments at which the calling thread waits, shows the readiness mechanism of `epoll` with a C server and a Java NIO server that were run on the build machine, and connects the results to Tomcat, Netty and Kafka.

### Concept and mechanism

#### The two phases of an input operation

Every input operation has two phases: waiting until data is available (the kernel receives a packet or a disk block into its buffer) and copying the data from the kernel buffer into the buffer of the process. The models differ in what the calling thread does during each phase.

rows: call returns `EAGAIN` at once; the program polls
one thread blocked on many descriptors
kernel performs the copy; completion is reported

blocks.text:
The word asynchronous is often misused. A non-blocking read with `epoll` is not asynchronous in the strict sense: the thread still performs the copy and decides when to read. In a truly asynchronous interface the thread submits the operation and the kernel completes it, including the copy. The distinction is irrelevant for most Java programs but is answered in interviews.

#### Blocking I/O and thread per connection

The simplest server accepts a connection and assigns a thread to it; the thread calls `read`, which blocks until data arrives. The code is sequential and easy to reason about, and the kernel schedules the threads. The cost is one thread per connection: each carries a stack (the default `-Xss` is 1 MiB of virtual address space on Linux x86-64, committed on use), kernel structures and a scheduling entry. With a few hundred connections this is acceptable. With tens of thousands of mostly idle connections the memory and the context switches become the limit, and the thread count itself is a risk (the thread explosion incident in the Part on processes, threads and scheduling).

#### Readiness: select, poll and epoll

A multiplexing call blocks one thread until any one of many descriptors is ready for reading or writing. Three system calls provide it:

- `select` takes bit sets of descriptors with a hard limit of `FD_SETSIZE` (1024) and rescans all of them on every call.
- `poll` takes an array of descriptors without that limit but still copies the whole array into the kernel and scans it on every call.
- `epoll` keeps the interest list inside the kernel. `epoll_ctl` adds and removes descriptors once; `epoll_wait` returns only the descriptors that are ready.

The cost of `select` and `poll` grows with the number of registered descriptors on every call, while the cost of `epoll_wait` grows with the number of ready descriptors.

blocks.text: Inside the kernel an `epoll` instance has two structures. The interest list is a red-black tree keyed by descriptor, so adding and removing costs O(log n). The ready list is a linked list that the kernel appends to from a callback when a registered socket receives data. `epoll_wait` copies the entries of the ready list to the caller and sleeps if the list is empty.

blocks.text:
`epoll` supports two trigger modes. In level-triggered mode (the default), a descriptor is reported as long as unread data remains, which makes the loop simple and safe. In edge-triggered mode (`EPOLLET`) a descriptor is reported once per arrival of new data and the program must read until `EAGAIN`; it reduces wake-ups but is easy to get wrong. Regular files are always reported as ready, so `epoll` helps for sockets, pipes and timers but not for disk files; this is why disk I/O in event-loop servers is moved to worker threads.

#### Asynchronous I/O and io_uring

Linux AIO (`io_submit`) is limited to files opened with `O_DIRECT` and has been rarely used outside databases. `io_uring`, available since Linux 5.1, supplies two ring buffers shared between user space and the kernel: a submission queue to which the program appends operation descriptions (read, write, accept, send, fsync) and a completion queue from which it reads results. Submission and completion need few or no system calls in steady state. It supports files and sockets uniformly. The JDK does not use `io_uring`; Netty offers an incubating transport for it. `io_uring` was not exercised on the build machine, so the description here is based on the kernel documentation only.

Java's `AsynchronousFileChannel` on Linux is implemented with a thread pool that performs ordinary blocking calls, and `AsynchronousSocketChannel` uses `epoll` with a pool of threads, so neither is kernel-level asynchronous I/O.

#### Zero-copy transfers

A conventional file-to-socket transfer in a loop of `read` and `write` copies data twice through user space: from the page cache into a user buffer, then from the buffer into a socket buffer. The `sendfile` call instructs the kernel to move the data between the two descriptors without the round trip to user space. `mmap` maps the page cache into the address space of the process so that reads need no copy into a separate buffer, and `splice` moves data between descriptors through a pipe.

blocks.text:
In Java, `FileChannel.transferTo` uses `sendfile` where the kernel supports it, and `FileChannel.map` returns a `MappedByteBuffer`. Apache Kafka stores each partition as segment files and serves consumers by `transferTo` from the page cache to the socket, so that a record that a consumer reads shortly after it was written never enters the JVM heap. The advantage disappears when TLS is enabled between broker and client, because the data must be encrypted in user space.

### Worked trace: an epoll echo server

The server in the listing is a complete single-threaded echo server. It registers the listening socket with `epoll`, accepts all pending connections when the listening socket is ready and echoes data from every ready client socket.

blocks.text: The client is a short Python script that opens N connections, sends one line on each and checks the echo:

blocks.caption: The server sleeps in epoll_wait and wakes only for the listening socket or for ready clients; one wake-up handled two clients, and the EAGAIN on the third accept shows that the backlog was drained.
blocks.alt: Client(s) Kernel epoll_echo | python epoll + TCP single thread | epoll_create1(0) = 4; epoll_ctl(4, ADD, 3) | 2 x connect() | epoll_wait(4,[fd 3 EPOLLIN]) = 1 | accept(3) = 5; epoll_ctl(ADD, 5); accept(3) = 6; ADD 6 | accept(3) = -1 EAGAIN (backlog drained) | send hello-0, hello-1 | epoll_wait(4,[fd 5, fd 6]) = 2 | read(5) = 8; write(5, 8); read(6) = 8; write(6, 8) | close() | epoll_wait(4,[fd 5]) = 1; read(5) = 0 (EOF); close(5)

blocks.text:
1. The descriptors 0 to 2 exist already; the listening socket takes descriptor 3 and the `epoll` instance descriptor 4.
2. The first `epoll_wait` returns the listening socket (descriptor 3) because two connections are pending. The loop calls `accept` until it returns `EAGAIN`; the accepted sockets receive descriptors 5 and 6 and are added to the interest list.
3. The next `epoll_wait` returns both client sockets in a single call (`= 2`). One system call served two connections, which is how a single thread scales: the number of wake-ups depends on bursts, not on connections.
4. After a client closes, `read` returns 0 (end of file) and the server closes the descriptor; closing removes it from the interest list.
5. With 200 clients connected, the server had 205 descriptors (3 standard, listener, epoll instance and 200 sockets) and `Threads: 1` in `/proc/PID/status`.

### Hands-on

#### The same design in Java NIO

The Java `Selector` is an `epoll` instance on Linux. The listing implements the same echo protocol; the program prints the implementation class to show that.

blocks.title: NioEcho.java

blocks.text: The loop has the structure of the C program: one blocking call, then a dispatch on the ready keys. The `while` `(buf.hasRemaining())` write loop is a simplification; a production server registers `OP_WRITE` and keeps a per-connection output buffer, because a non-blocking write may accept only part of the data.

$ grep -E "VmRSS|Threads" /proc/$JP/status

Threads:        19
blocks.title: 500 connections served by one selector thread (JDK 21, typical output)

blocks.text: The 19 threads are the JVM's own: the main thread, garbage collector and compiler workers, the signal dispatcher and so on. None was added for the 500 connections. A blocking design with one platform thread per connection would have needed 500 more, each with a stack reservation of 1 MiB of address space.

blocks.text:
#### How the Java frameworks map onto the models

Tomcat in its default NIO connector (the one Spring Boot embeds) has an acceptor thread that accepts connections, one or more poller threads that run a `Selector` over idle connections and a worker pool that executes the servlet. A request waits in the poller until bytes arrive; a worker then runs the controller to completion and blocks on every database or HTTP call it makes. The relevant Spring Boot properties are `server.tomcat.threads.max` (default 200 workers), `server.tomcat.max-connections` (default 8192 open connections) and `server.tomcat.accept-count` (default 100 queued connections beyond that). Concurrency in this design is limited by the worker pool, not by the number of connections.

Netty, and Reactor Netty underneath Spring WebFlux, run an event loop per thread, each owning a `Selector`; a connection is bound to one loop for its life. The loops are few (twice the core count for plain Netty by default). The code on a loop must never block, because a blocked loop stops every connection assigned to it. With Java 21 virtual threads, blocking socket calls park the virtual thread and the JDK waits for readiness with an `epoll` poller internally, giving the blocking programming style on top of the multiplexing model.

### Real-world incidents

#### Incident: a blocking call stalls every connection of an event loop

**Scenario.** A reactive gateway built on Netty validates requests by calling a licence database synchronously from the handler. After a database slowdown, latency of all clients, including those that never touch the licence check, rises from milliseconds to seconds.

**Symptoms.** CPU is nearly idle, the number of open connections grows and request timeouts occur for unrelated endpoints. Health checks served by the same loops time out and the orchestrator restarts healthy pods.

**Diagnosis.** A thread dump shows the event-loop threads, not the workers, sitting in a blocking call. The reproduction replaced the handler of `NioEcho` with one that sleeps two seconds when a message begins with the letter `s`, which stands in for a slow database call, and measured a second client.

import socket, sys, time
port = int(sys.argv[1])
a = socket.create_connection(("127.0.0.1", port))
b = socket.create_connection(("127.0.0.1", port))
t0 = time.time()
a.sendall(b"slow-request\n")
time.sleep(0.1)

blocks.text:
The fast request, sent 100 ms after the slow one on a different connection, was answered after 1906 ms: it waited for the loop thread to finish the 2000 ms call. The thread that owns the loop is in a sleeping or waiting state and uses 0.0 percent CPU, which explains why CPU graphs look healthy during the incident. In a real service the frame at the top of the stack would be a JDBC or blocking HTTP client method, which is the line to search for.

**Root cause.** Blocking work was executed on a thread whose only duty is to multiplex many connections. Every connection assigned to that loop waited for it.

**Fix.** Immediate: restart does not help; reduce the dependency timeout or bypass the check. Permanent: move blocking calls to a bounded worker pool (in Netty an `EventExecutorGroup`, in Reactor `publishOn(Schedulers.boundedElastic())`) or replace them with a non-blocking client; set timeouts on every outbound call. On Java 21, a virtual thread per request removes the restriction because blocking parks only that virtual thread.

**Prevention.** Run a blocking-call detector in tests (BlockHound for Reactor), alert on event-loop lag or pending-task counts, and keep the health endpoint independent of dependencies on the same loop.

### Questions to expect

#### What is the difference between blocking and non-blocking I/O?

A blocking call suspends the thread until the operation can complete; a non-blocking call returns immediately with `EAGAIN` when it cannot. Non-blocking calls are combined with a readiness mechanism so that the program does not spin.

#### What is the difference between synchronous and asynchronous I/O?

In synchronous I/O (blocking, non-blocking and multiplexing) the calling thread performs the data transfer itself. In asynchronous I/O the program submits the operation and the kernel completes it, copy included, and signals completion.

#### Why is `epoll` more scalable than `select` and `poll`?

`select` and `poll` pass the entire descriptor set on every call and scan it, so the cost is proportional to the number of descriptors. `epoll` keeps the interest list in the kernel and returns only ready descriptors, so the cost is proportional to the number of events.

#### What is the difference between level-triggered and edge-triggered `epoll`?

Level-triggered reports a descriptor as long as it remains ready; edge-triggered reports only when its state changes and requires the program to read until `EAGAIN`. Edge-triggered reduces wake-ups but is easier to misuse.

#### Why does epoll not help for regular files?

Regular files are always reported as ready, so readiness carries no information. Event-loop frameworks run file I/O on separate threads.

#### How many threads does a Tomcat server need for 10000 idle keep-alive connections?

Few: the poller threads watch the idle sockets through a selector; a worker thread is used only while a request is processed. The number of workers (default 200) limits concurrent requests, and `max-connections` (default 8192) limits open connections.

#### What does `sendfile` do, and where is it used in Java?

It transfers data from a file descriptor to a socket inside the kernel, avoiding copies through user space. `FileChannel.transferTo` uses it, and Kafka relies on it to serve consumers from the page cache.

#### Why must code on a Netty event loop not block?

One loop thread serves many connections; a blocked thread delays all of them, as the reproduction showed with a 1906 ms delay for an unrelated request.

#### What is `io_uring`?

A Linux interface with shared submission and completion rings for asynchronous operations on files and sockets, which reduces system calls and supports real asynchronous completion.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
Key points

- Every input has a wait phase and a copy phase; blocking, non-blocking, multiplexing, signal-driven and asynchronous models differ in who waits during each.
- `epoll` registers descriptors once and returns only ready ones; one thread served 500 connections in a JVM with 19 threads, and one C thread served 200.
- Zero-copy (`sendfile`, `mmap`) removes user-space copies; Kafka depends on it, TLS defeats it.
- Tomcat uses pollers plus a worker pool; Netty binds each connection to one event loop; blocking on a loop stalls every connection it owns.
- Virtual threads in Java 21 keep the blocking style while the JDK multiplexes underneath.

sections.title: Logging and Log Rotation in Production

blocks.text:
Logs are the file workload that production systems produce continuously and that nobody plans disk capacity for. A log file is written by one process, read by others, rotated by a third and deleted by a fourth, and each of these actors interacts with the file system semantics of the previous chapters: names versus inodes, open descriptors, ordered writes, synchronous cost. Failures in this area are among the most frequent operational incidents: the disk fills up, the space does not return after cleanup, the log disappears after rotation, or the service slows down because logging blocks.

### Concept and mechanism

#### Where logs go

A Java service can send log events to a file, to standard output, to a network collector or to the system journal. The choices carry different failure modes.

rows: Logback `RollingFileAppender` or Log4j2 with its own rolling policy
disk full without a size cap, blocking when the disk is slow
writer keeps the old inode, or lines lost at truncation
the runtime captures the stream into a file on the node and rotates it
node disk fills if the runtime limits are absent; `kubectl logs` loses rotated data
structured binary journal written by `systemd-journald`, read with `journalctl`
rate limiting drops messages, journal size limits discard the oldest
blocking or loss when the collector is down
blocks.caption: Log destinations and their failure modes.

blocks.text:
#### Rotation: rename versus truncate

A process that writes a log keeps a descriptor to the inode. Rotation must therefore decide what happens to that descriptor. Two strategies exist, and the experiment below used the same Java writer under both.

- **Rename and signal.** The rotating tool renames `app.log` to `app.log.1` and tells the process to reopen the path (a postrotate command such as `kill -HUP`, or a `create` directive for a new empty file). The renamed file keeps being written until the process reopens, because the descriptor follows the inode, not the name. Without the signal, the process writes to `app.log.1` forever and the new `app.log` stays empty.
- **Copy and truncate** (`copytruncate` in `logrotate`). The tool copies the file and truncates the original to zero length while the process keeps writing to it. No signal is needed, but the lines written between the copy and the truncate are lost, and the writer must have opened the file in append mode (`O_APPEND`) or its offset will leave a hole of zeros at the old position.

Java logging frameworks avoid both problems by rotating inside the process: Logback's `SizeAndTimeBasedRollingPolicy` and Log4j2's rolling policies close the old file and open the new one themselves. Spring Boot exposes `logging.logback.rollingpolicy.max-file-size` (default 10 MB), `max-history` (default 7) and `total-size-cap` (default 0, which means no cap and should be set explicitly).

blocks.text:
#### Deleted but open files

When a log file is deleted while a process holds it open, the directory entry disappears but the inode and its blocks remain until the last descriptor is closed. The process continues to write, the file keeps growing and no tool that walks directories can see it. This produces the situation in which `df` reports a full disk and `du` finds nothing to account for the space.

blocks.text:
The reverse view is a recovery technique: the deleted file is still reachable as `/proc/PID/fd/N`, so its contents can be copied out or truncated in place.

#### Journald and container logs

On systems with systemd, a service started as a unit writes standard output and standard error to the journal, which is queried with `journalctl -u NAME`, with options `-f` (follow), `--since`, `-p err` (priority) and `-o json`. The size of the journal is bounded by `SystemMaxUse` and `SystemKeepFree` in `journald.conf`, and the rate by `RateLimitIntervalSec` and `RateLimitBurst`; a service that logs in bursts can lose messages without any error. The build machine did not use systemd as its init system (PID 1 was a process-management shim), so `journalctl` output cannot be shown and the journald statements follow the manual pages.

For containers the convention is to log to standard output and let the platform handle the files. Docker's default `json-file` driver stores the stream on the host and has no size limit unless `--log-opt max-size` and `max-file` are set. Kubernetes writes container logs under `/var/log/pods` on the node and the kubelet rotates them (the settings `containerLogMaxSize` and `containerLogMaxFiles`, 10 MiB and 5 by default).

#### The cost of logging

A log call is a write. With a file appender it ends in a `write` call of a few hundred bytes, which is cheap while the page cache absorbs it and expensive when a thread must wait. Three situations make logging slow: a synchronous appender on a slow or saturated disk (every request thread blocks), a flush after every event (`immediateFlush` set to `true` costs one system call per event, but not an `fsync`) and a very high log level on a busy path. Asynchronous appenders (Logback `AsyncAppender`, Log4j2 asynchronous loggers) decouple the request thread from the write by a bounded queue; the policy for a full queue (block, drop) must be chosen deliberately.

### Worked trace: what happens to a log file that is renamed and deleted

The test used `LogWriter.java`, which appends one kilobyte lines at a fixed rate through a `PrintWriter` opened in append mode.

blocks.title: LogWriter.java

blocks.code:
$ java LogWriter.java /logfs/var/log/app/app.log 100 &
$ ls -l /logfs/var/log/app
-rw-r--r-- 1 root root 192800 Oct 18 02:18 app.log
$ mv app.log app.log.1; sleep 2; ls -l; ls -l /proc/$JP/fd | grep log
-rw-r--r-- 1 root root 385600 Oct 18 02:18 app.log.1
l-wx------ 1 root root 64 Oct 18 02:18 4 -> /logfs/var/log/app/app.log.1
$ cp app.log.1 app.log.2; : > app.log.1; sleep 2; ls -l
-rw-r--r-- 1 root root 192800 Oct 18 02:18 app.log.1
-rw-r--r-- 1 root root 385600 Oct 18 02:18 app.log.2
blocks.title: Rename without a signal, then copy and truncate (writer rate 100 lines per second)

blocks.text:
After the `mv`, no file named `app.log` existed and the file kept growing under the new name, from 192800 to 385600 bytes; descriptor 4 of the process pointed to `app.log.1`. After the copy and truncate, `app.log.1` started again from zero and had grown back to 192800 bytes after two seconds, while `app.log.2` held the earlier 385600 bytes. Any lines written between `cp` and `: >` were in neither file. Because the writer opened the file with `O_APPEND`, no hole appeared.

The inode number 13 and the link count 0 identify the file; `SIZE/OFF` of 11568000 bytes matches the 12 MiB difference between `df` and `du`. The size kept growing by about a megabyte per second while the directory was empty.

### Real-world incidents

#### Incident: disk full because a deleted log file is still open

**Scenario.** A disk alert fires on a service host at 95 percent. An operator removes the large `app.log` and sees no change in `df`. The service writes to a 56 MiB volume in the reproduction; in production the volume is far larger and the effect is identical.

**Symptoms.** `df` stays high or keeps growing; `du -sh` on the mount point reports a few kilobytes; `ls` shows no large file; writes begin to fail with `No space left on device` later.

**Diagnosis.** The sign is a disagreement between `df` and `du`. The commands are the ones of the decision tree in the file system chapter.

COMMAND  PID USER  FD  TYPE DEVICE SIZE/OFF NLINK NODE NAME

-rw-r--r-- 1 root root 15424000 Oct 18 02:17 /backup/recovered.log

/dev/loop0       56M   15M   37M  29% /logfs
$ : > /proc/4177/fd/4; sleep 1; df -h /logfs | tail -1

blocks.text:
**Root cause.** The file was removed by name while a process still held it open. The kernel keeps the inode until the last descriptor closes, so the blocks stayed allocated and the writer continued to add to them.

**Fix.** Immediate: truncate in place with `: > /proc/PID/fd/N`, which frees the blocks without restarting the process (after copying out the content if it is needed); or restart or signal the service so that it reopens its log. Permanent: never delete an active log; truncate it (`: > file`) or rotate it with a mechanism the writer cooperates with.

**Prevention.** Alert on the difference between `df` and the sum of `du` (or on `lsof +L1` returning large entries) and on file system usage with a margin that gives time to react. Cap the log size in the framework (`total-size-cap`) so that no log can fill a volume.

#### Incident: a log flood fills the disk

**Scenario.** A release enables `DEBUG` logging for a package to investigate a defect and the change is not reverted. Under production traffic the service writes tens of megabytes per second.

**Symptoms.** The disk fills within minutes. The service begins to fail writes and the host cannot create temporary files, so unrelated components fail as well. In the reproduction a writer producing 20 MB per second filled a 56 MiB volume within about three seconds.

**Diagnosis.** The questions are which volume, which directory and which file, and whether the growth continues.

blocks.code:
$ df -h /logfs | tail -1
/dev/loop0       56M   55M     0 100% /logfs
$ du -xh --max-depth=3 /logfs | sort -rh | head -4
55M     /logfs/var/log/app
55M     /logfs/var/log
55M     /logfs/var
55M     /logfs
$ ls -lh /logfs/var/log/app
total 55M
-rw-r--r-- 1 root root 55M Oct 18 02:18 debug.log
blocks.title: The volume and the offending file (build machine; volume 56 MiB)

blocks.text:
The volume is at 100 percent and the directory listing identifies a single file, `debug.log`, which accounts for the whole usage; the log level setting of the service confirms the cause.

**Root cause.** A log level change multiplied the log volume by several orders of magnitude, and nothing bounded the size of the log file or reserved space for the rest of the system.

**Fix.** Immediate: lower the level at runtime (Spring Boot Actuator `POST /actuator/loggers/PACKAGE` with `{"configuredLevel": "INFO"}`, or the JMX operation of the logging framework), then free space by truncating the file (`: > debug.log`) rather than deleting it while the process runs, as the previous incident showed. Permanent: configure a size-based rolling policy with a total cap, put logs on a separate volume or in a container with an `ephemeral-storage` limit, and require a change record and an expiry for temporary debug levels. **Prevention.** Alert on the rate of growth of the log volume (bytes per minute), not only on the percentage used. Sample or rate-limit repetitive messages. Keep the disk that hosts the log separate from the one that hosts the application or the database.

#### Incident: accidental removal of a file that a process has open

**Scenario.** An operator cleaning a data directory removes `pricing.csv`, a lookup table that a long-running process keeps open. The process continues to work, but a restart would fail and no backup of the latest version exists.

**Symptoms.** The file no longer appears in `ls`. The service still answers, since it holds a descriptor. After a planned restart the service would fail to load its configuration.

**Diagnosis and recovery.** While the process runs, the content is still reachable. The reproduction used a `sleep` process that holds the file as its standard input, which is an open descriptor like any other.

blocks.code:
$ md5sum pricing.csv
9f3248a1cbf2e5be3d6309d4456b375f  pricing.csv
$ (sleep 120 < pricing.csv & echo $! > pid)
$ rm pricing.csv; ls
pid
$ ls -l /proc/$(cat pid)/fd/0
lr-x------ 1 root root 64 Oct 18 02:35 /proc/15496/fd/0 -> /tmp/osw_o5/rm_test/pricing.csv (deleted)
$ cp /proc/$(cat pid)/fd/0 pricing.csv; md5sum pricing.csv
9f3248a1cbf2e5be3d6309d4456b375f  pricing.csv
blocks.title: Recovery through /proc (build machine)

blocks.text:
The checksum of the recovered file equals the original. The method works only while the descriptor is open and only for the part of the file that exists on disk; if the process has already exited, the blocks are free and only forensic tools or backups remain, with poor results on ext4.

**Root cause.** A removal by name on a file in use, without a backup or a snapshot.

**Fix.** Copy the file from `/proc/PID/fd/N` immediately, verify the checksum, restore the name and only then restart anything. Do not close or restart the holding process before the copy.

**Prevention.** Keep configuration and data under version control or in a backed-up volume; use snapshots (LVM, ZFS, cloud volume snapshots) before cleanups; run cleanups with `find ... -print` first, then `-delete`; restrict write permission of production directories so that ordinary operators cannot delete application data.

### Questions to expect

#### Why does the free space not increase after a log file is deleted?

The process that writes the log still holds an open descriptor, so the inode and blocks are retained until it closes the file. `lsof +L1` lists such files, and truncating through `/proc/PID/fd/N` or restarting the process releases the space.

**What is the difference between \`logrotate\` with \`copytruncate\` and rotation with a signal?** With a signal the file is renamed and the process reopens the path, which loses nothing but requires cooperation. With `copytruncate` the file is copied and truncated in place; no cooperation is needed but lines written between the copy and the truncate are lost.

#### Why does a service keep writing to `app.log.1` after rotation?

A descriptor refers to an inode, not to a name. After a rename the descriptor still refers to the renamed file, until the process reopens the path.

#### Where should a containerised Java service write its logs?

To standard output, so that the runtime collects and rotates them with configured limits. Logging to a file inside the writable layer costs copy-on-write overhead and disappears with the container.

#### How can logging slow a service down?

A synchronous appender blocks request threads when the disk or the collector is slow. An asynchronous appender with a bounded queue decouples them, but the policy for a full queue (block or drop) must be defined.

#### How is a disk-full condition diagnosed quickly?

`df -h` for the volume, `df -i` for inodes, `du -xh --max-depth=N` for the directory, `lsof +L1` for deleted open files. The disagreement between `df` and `du` points to open deleted files.

#### How can a deleted file that a process has open be recovered?

Copy it from `/proc/PID/fd/N` while the process is running. The kernel keeps the inode alive as long as the descriptor is open.

#### Which limits should bound logs in production?

The framework (`max-file-size`, `max-history`, `total-size-cap`), the runtime for container logs (`max-size`, `max-file`, kubelet limits) and the journal (`SystemMaxUse`), plus a volume or ephemeral-storage limit as the last barrier.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
Key points

- A writer holds an inode, not a name: renaming does not redirect it and deleting does not free space while it is open.
- `df` greater than `du` means deleted-but-open files; `lsof +L1` finds them, `cp` or `: >` on `/proc/PID/fd/N` recovers or frees them without a restart.
- Rotate inside the framework or with a signal; `copytruncate` can lose lines; containers log to standard output with runtime-enforced limits.
- Bound every log: `total-size-cap`, rolling policy, separate volume, alert on growth rate.
- Logging is I/O on the request path unless it is asynchronous; size the queue and decide the full-queue policy.
